sub_unit_name: Corrosion control methods - Cathodic protection - Sacrificial anode and impressed current methods

content.title: Corrosion Control
content.description: Corrosion control involves methods that prevent or reduce the deterioration of metals. Cathodic protection is one of the most effective electrochemical methods used to protect metal structures.

content.content: Corrosion can be controlled by coatings, inhibitors, proper material selection, and cathodic protection. In cathodic protection, the metal to be protected is made the cathode, thereby preventing its oxidation.

content.title: Key Principle
content.content: Cathodic protection prevents corrosion by forcing the metal structure to act as the cathode of an electrochemical cell.

In cathodic protection, electrons are supplied to the metal surface so that oxidation does not occur. This method is widely used for underground pipelines, storage tanks, marine structures, and ship hulls.
In this method, a more active metal such as magnesium, zinc, or aluminium is connected to the metal structure. The active metal acts as the anode and corrodes instead of the protected structure.

In the impressed current method, an external DC power source supplies electrons to the metal structure. An inert anode such as graphite or platinum is used, making this method suitable for protecting large structures.

items.question: Underground Pipelines
items.answer: Protected from soil corrosion using cathodic protection.

items.question: Ship Hulls
items.answer: Sacrificial zinc anodes prevent seawater corrosion.

items.question: Storage Tanks
items.answer: Impressed current systems protect large steel tanks.

items.question: Marine Structures
items.answer: Cathodic protection increases service life in seawater environments.

content.title: Engineering Importance
content.content: Cathodic protection significantly extends the life of pipelines, bridges, ships, storage tanks, and offshore structures while reducing maintenance costs.
